title: History's a Mystery
pages: Book p.60 to 69 · Workbook p.48 to 55

learn.title: Welcome to Unit 6: History's a Mystery!
lines: In this unit you will:
🏺 learn words about archaeology: tombs, mummies, treasure and artifacts
🔎 use the passive voice: was found, were discovered
🕵️ say who did it with by: The mummy was found by hikers.
🎵 sing a song, 📖 read about the lost city of Atlantis, 🏛️ learn about local history, ✍️ write with examples

learn.title: Look at the big photo
lines: Open your book to pages 60 and 61.
This is Chichén Itzá in Yucatan, Mexico. It is a very old building made by the Maya people.
It looks like a pyramid. It is big and it has steps on every side.

learn.title: What is a mystery?
lines: A mystery is something that we cannot explain. We don't know the answer yet.
History is full of mysteries! Who built this? Why? How did they do it?
examples: Nobody knows how it was built.

sections.title: Vocabulary 1: Amazing Discoveries
sections.pages: Book p.62 to 63 · Workbook p.48 to 49

learn.title: Discoveries tell us about the past
lines: Archaeologists dig in the ground to find old things.
Each discovery helps us learn how people lived long ago.

learn.title: Three discoveries (short summary)
lines: Read the full texts on pages 62 and 63 in your book.
🇨🇳 210 BCE: A Chinese ruler, Qin Shihuang, was buried in a tomb with more than 6,000 statues: soldiers, dancers, acrobats and horses. The tomb is not completely excavated yet.
🇵🇪 450 CE: A female mummy was found in a tomb in Peru. She was beautifully preserved, with tattoos of snakes and spiders.
🇬🇧 650 CE: Treasure was found in a field in England in 2009. Later, more than 3,500 objects and lots of gold were discovered. Who buried it? Nobody knows.

learn.title: BCE and CE
lines: BCE = before the common era (a long, long time ago). The numbers count down: 300 BCE, 200 BCE, 100 BCE.
CE = the common era. The numbers count up: 100 CE, 450 CE, 2026 CE.

sections.title: Grammar 1: Passive voice, simple past

learn.title: Active or passive?
lines: Active: the person who does the action comes first. Thieves stole the gold.
Passive: the thing that the action happens to comes first. The gold was stolen.
learn.note: Use the passive when you don't know (or don't care) who did the action.

learn.title: was / were + past participle
lines: I, he, she, it, one thing → was
we, you, they, many things → were

learn.title: Questions in the passive
lines: Move was / were to the front.
examples: Was it discovered near here? Yes, it was. / No, it wasn't.

learn.title: "I was born…" is passive!
lines: We always say I was born in 2014. Never "I born".

lines: 1. Find a site.
2. Dig and find artifacts.
3. Take a sample (a small piece).
4. Analyze it in a lab.
5. Do a DNA test to learn about the person's family.

sections.title: Grammar 2: Passive voice with by + agent

learn.title: Who did it? Add by + the person
lines: When we know who did the action, we add by + the person (the agent).
examples: Active: The hiker found the mummy.
Passive: The mummy was found by the hiker.

learn.title: From active to passive in 3 steps
lines: 1. Move the object to the front: the bottles
2. Add was / were + past participle: weren't found
3. Add by + the agent: by the divers
examples: The divers didn't find the bottles. → The bottles weren't found by the divers.

learn.title: The Iceman story
lines: In 1991, a mummy was discovered by hikers in the ice. He was called the "Iceman."
He was studied by scientists for ten years. In 2001, he was analyzed by Paul Gostner, who found an injury in his arm.
Now we know he was killed by someone. But who? He was born over 5,000 years ago, so we don't know!

learn.title: The Lost City of Atlantis 🌊
lines: Read the full text in your book. This is a short summary.
Atlantis was a "lost city." In the story, it was destroyed in one terrible night of fire and earthquakes, and it sank into the sea.
A famous man named Plato first told the story more than 2,000 years ago. He said Atlantis was full of gold, silver and amazing wildlife.
Many people have looked for it, but no artifacts have ever been found.
Most people think Atlantis was never a real place. It's probably just a story, but some people still hope it will be found one day.

learn.title: Trash Is Treasure (Workbook p.54)
lines: Read the full text in your workbook. This is a short summary.
There are many kinds of archaeologists:
🔬 Forensic archaeologists analyze DNA and help the police.
🗺️ Landscape archaeologists study sites.
🦴 Osteologists study bones.
🗑️ "Garbologists" study trash. Old trash shows what people threw away, what they ate and what diseases they had.

book.q: Have any artifacts from Atlantis been found?

book.q: What do most people think about Atlantis?
book.answer: They think it was never a real place. It's probably just a story.

learn.title: Our mission: Learn about local history 🏛️
lines: Local history is the history of the place where you live: your town, your temple, your market, your family.
When we learn about the past, we understand our home better, and we take care of old places.

learn.title: Johan Reinhard, National Geographic Explorer
lines: Johan Reinhard is an anthropologist. He studies people and how they lived in the past.
The photo shows him with a mummy on Mount Llullaillaco, Argentina.
His message: He wanted to learn about people from the past who lived very different lives. He was so happy to find a job that does this! Read his words on page 69. 📖

learn.title: How can I learn about local history?
lines: 👵 Ask your grandparents about the old days.
🛕 Visit an old temple or a museum near your home.
📷 Look at old photos of your town.
🚯 Don't write on or damage old buildings.

book.q: Is it important to protect historical places in your country? Why or why not?
book.answer: Yes, it is, because they tell us about our past, and when they are destroyed, they are lost forever.

book.q: What do you think we can learn from people who lived in ancient times?
book.answer: We can learn how they built houses, what they ate, and how they lived without phones and cars.

book.q: Which places are of historical interest in your area?
book.answer: There is a very old temple and an old market near my school.
book.hint: Think of old temples, museums, old markets or old houses near you.

sections.title: Writing: Exemplification

learn.title: Writing with examples
lines: In exemplification writing, you give examples to support your important ideas.
Examples show the reader that you know what you are writing about.

learn.title: Words that introduce examples
examples: Archaeologists find many things, such as pottery, coins and statues.
table: ตัวอย่างเช่น

learn.title: Memories from the Past (short summary)
lines: Read the full text in your workbook. 📒
New discoveries tell us about the past. A good example is the Iceman, found in 1991 by hikers in the Alps.
The Peruvian mummy also tells us a lot. For instance, she was probably 12 to 14 years old, and she had strong bones and great teeth.

learn.title: Plan: The terra-cotta statues
lines: 1. Main idea: The terra-cotta statues tell us a lot about the past.
2. Example: For instance, there are more than 6,000 statues, such as soldiers, horses and acrobats.
3. Example: Specifically, each statue has a different face.
4. End: Say why the discovery is amazing.

wb.q: Read "Memories from the Past." Underline all the expressions that refer to examples.
wb.answer: A good example is · namely · For instance · Specifically
wb.hint: There are 4 expressions. Look for the words in the list at the top of the page.

wb.q: Write about the terra-cotta statues. What does this discovery tell us about the past? Use examples.
wb.answer: The terra-cotta statues tell us a lot about the past. A good example is the army of soldiers. There are more than 6,000 statues, such as soldiers, horses and acrobats. Specifically, each statue has a different face. This tells us that the workers were very skilled.
wb.hint: Use the plan in Learn. Use at least two example words.
